talks.title: Michael Whitehead - Securing Values: The Ethics of Cyber Security
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Michael Whitehead - Securing Values: The Ethics of Cyber Security.
talks.summary:
Ethics in Security Work

Michael Whitehead, a University of Leeds security engineer, argues ethics shape every investigation. Becoming a parent shifted his priorities and sharpened his view of professional responsibility beyond technical capability.

Investigation Boundaries

HR requests to probe staff misconduct require documented scope, legal and HR buy-in, and clarity on monitoring authority. Without limits, analysts risk overreach, lawsuits, and harm—including a case where overwhelming evidence contributed to an early-career employee taking their own life.

Phishing Simulation Ethics

Phishing exercises are acceptable when aimed at education, not humiliation. Whitehead criticizes simulations dangling financial rewards during COVID-era job fear, citing Chicago Tribune and GoDaddy emails that exploited real anxiety. Defenders must draw ethical lines attackers will not.

Broader Themes

He warns against confirmation bias, cautions that ability to act does not imply permission, and invites discussion on balancing security duties with human cost.

talks.title: Liam Follin - How to get away with hacking
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Liam Follin - How to get away with hacking.
talks.summary:
Personal Journey

KPMG lead pentester Liam Follin recounts moving from martial arts instructor and Costa barista to CHECK team leader, framing the talk as practical guidance for breaking into penetration testing rather than elite CTF gatekeeping.

Technical Foundations (Without Elitism)

He recommends OverTheWire Bandit, basic coding, TryHackMe or Hack The Box, and PortSwigger for app testing—not to top leaderboards but to pass hiring CTFs. He demos turning a reflected XSS blocked by JSON encoding into cookie theft using JavaScript string.fromCharCode and jQuery callbacks.

Non-Technical Essentials

Follin stresses meticulous note-taking (Obsidian linked to GitHub), conference networking that led to his KPMG role, and accepting that pentesting involves travel, exams (CHECK, CSTL, CBEST), extensive reporting, and continuous learning across ever-growing tech stacks.

Industry Realities

Entry is competitive—seventy applicants in days for one junior role—and success requires sustained effort beyond nine-to-five, but specialization beats pretending to master every domain.

talks.title: Hack Glasgow 2025: Lennaert Oudshoorn
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Lennaert Oudshoorn - Getting started in bug bounty....
talks.summary:
Bug bounty basics

Intigriti Head of Triage Lennaert Oudshoorn explains bug bounty as paid vulnerability disclosure across web, mobile, hardware, and more—usually a side hustle, not a quick path to millions. Motivations include learning, community, and career stories like hunters hired after platform success.

Hunting styles

Hunt wide via OSINT, certificate transparency, and automation to find forgotten assets (admin panels, S3 buckets, subdomain takeovers). Hunt deep on one app for logic bugs and IDORs—lower volume but higher impact and fewer duplicates. Mix both approaches.

Programs and reports

Beginners should avoid hyper-competitive programs like Google; try newer scope, lower bounties, or VDPs. Read rules of engagement for legal safe harbor. Good reports need clear titles, realistic severity, reproducible steps—not open-port scans. Triage teams want valid bugs, not rejections.

talks.title: maya boeckh - Yelling at the people and/or the thinking sand isn't helping
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning maya boeckh - Yelling at the people and/or the thinking sand isn't helping.
talks.summary:
## A Burnt-Out Industry Rant

Maya Boeckh delivers a candid Hack Glasgow talk about cybersecurity culture, burnout, and the gap between shiny tools and how organizations actually work. She speaks from personal exhaustion, having pushed through health issues to present.

## Documentation vs. Reality

Teams rarely understand their own systems—archives run untouched since 2003, surviving outages by accident until something breaks and nobody knows how to fix it. Learning is discouraged when KPIs demand tickets closed faster than engineers can research root causes.

## AI Hype Adds Noise

Boeckh skewers the flood of "AI" and ChatGPT references at conferences while fundamentals remain broken. Vendors sell thinking sand solutions to problems that need staffing, clarity, and sustainable pace—not another dashboard.

## Burnout Is the Default

She argues nearly everyone in security will burn out at least once. Constant information overload inside and outside the industry leaves no room to adapt. Her closing plea: individuals cannot absorb every organizational failure, and the community should stop building dystopian "torment nexus" products without questioning who pays the human cost.
